headline: The Lie of Starting Over, Filmed Twice by Edward Yang
lede: A brief exchange on X pairs two films by the Taiwanese director Edward Yang — *Taipei Story* (1985) and *Yi Yi* (2000) — as essential viewing for anyone in their twenties reckoning with the discovery that no amount of reinvention dissolves the problem of being oneself. Both are among the most celebrated works in world cinema, and together they form a sustained, two-part argument about identity's resistance to external remedy.
body:
The two films are *Taipei Story* (1985) and *Yi Yi* (2000), both directed by Edward Yang — the Taiwanese filmmaker considered among the finest directors of the late twentieth century. That both come from the same hand, fifteen years apart, is the key to the recommendation: they are companion works, returning to the same predicament at different temperatures.

*Taipei Story* is Yang's second feature. Its protagonist, Ah-chen, is a young Taipei professional who dreams of emigrating to America; her childhood boyfriend Ah-lung is a former baseball prodigy who cannot release the person he once was. **The film states its thesis aloud:** “Forget America. It's not a panacea either. Like marriage, it's just a fleeting hope, giving you a kind of illusion that you can start everything over again.” The @ctrlarchive account's caption — “The illusion that you can start over. Just a fleeting hope” — is a near-direct quotation from this line, which is how *Taipei Story* is identified as the second film the thread discusses. The film ends without consolation.

*Yi Yi* is Yang's final film, made in 2000, seven years before his death from a heart attack. At 173 minutes it follows a single Taipei family through a wedding and a funeral, each member navigating a private crisis invisible to the others. The father, NJ, reunites abroad with his first love and discovers, gently, that he is who he is now — no recoverable earlier version of himself exists. His eight-year-old son, Yang-Yang, photographs the backs of strangers' heads because, he explains, people cannot see the parts of themselves they cannot look at directly. The film won Best Director at the Cannes Film Festival in 2000 and appears on most canonical lists of the greatest films of the twenty-first century.

Together they argue that identity resists external remedy. *Taipei Story* states the case harshly: geography, romance, and the dream of emigration change nothing, and may make things worse. *Yi Yi* restates it with greater warmth — everyone in the family is lost simultaneously, and no one can quite see it in the others. The tweet's blunt phrase, “everyone's in the same shit,” is the plainest summary of what both films spend hours demonstrating with formal precision and considerable beauty. For a viewer still in the process of forming a self, the recognition is the point.

Both films are rooted in a Taipei caught between *Taiwan New Cinema*'s social-realist inheritance, Japanese cultural influence, and an American corporate modernity arriving in waves. The characters' identity crises are not purely personal: they are also the crisis of a society uncertain of what it is becoming — which is precisely why the films remain legible to viewers who have never set foot in Taiwan.

concepts.definition: A film movement that emerged in Taiwan in the early 1980s, characterized by naturalistic acting, location shooting, and stories drawn from working-class and provincial life. Directors Edward Yang and Hou Hsiao-hsien used it to examine Taiwan's rapid industrialization and shifting cultural identity. The movement is considered one of the most significant national cinema movements of the late twentieth century, influencing filmmakers across Asia and beyond.
